data.title: Publicly Exposed AWS Root Account Credentials in Client-Side JavaScript
data.summary: Imagur's public website serves a JavaScript file that embeds a live AWS access key and matching secret for the AWS root account that owns the application's cloud environment. Any visitor can read the credentials directly from the browser and immediately gain full administrative control of the Imagur AWS account.
data.description:
The file `https://imagesharer.xyz/js/awsvalid.js` is a public static JavaScript asset. Lines 3-7 contain a commented-out block holding an AWS access key ID, matching secret, and region (ap-southeast-2). The access key ID begins with `AKIA...` and belongs to the root user of AWS account 016170038077.

Ownership was verified with a single read-only `aws sts get-caller-identity` call using the exposed credential, which returned:

```
UserId:  016170038077
Account: 016170038077
Arn:     arn:aws:iam::016170038077:root
```

Because the returned ARN ends in `:root`, this is NOT a scoped IAM user; it is the AWS account root user. Root credentials bypass all IAM policies and permission boundaries and allow an attacker to:

- Read, modify, or delete every resource in the account (S3 data, databases, EC2, IAM users, billing, DNS/Route53, CloudFront, backups).
- Create new IAM users and backdoors.
- Close the AWS account.
- Incur unbounded costs (crypto mining, data egress).
- Change billing/payment information and tax identity.

**Business impact.** Complete loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all data and services hosted in AWS account 016170038077; likely data breach affecting all users; possible full account takeover, destruction, or financial loss. Internet-wide bots continuously scrape for `AKIA`-prefixed strings, so exposure time (not just presence) drives risk — if the key has been online for any meaningful period it should be treated as already compromised.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p0-awskey/awsvalid.js` (full captured file)
- `evidence/p0-awskey/awsvalid.headers.txt` (HTTP 200, `text/javascript`)
- `evidence/p0-awskey/sts-get-caller-identity.json` (ownership verified)

*Note: The secret portion of the credential is deliberately not reproduced in this report.*
data.recommendation:
**Immediate (within hours):**

1. Log into the AWS Console as root and rotate the root access key: deactivate then delete the exposed key immediately (IAM -> Security credentials -> Access keys).
2. Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on the root user if not already enabled.
3. Review CloudTrail event history for AWS account 016170038077 for the last 90 days. Look for any API calls originating from unfamiliar IPs or using the leaked access key ID. Pay special attention to IAM, S3, EC2, and RDS activity.
4. Remove the credential block entirely from `awsvalid.js` and redeploy. Confirm it is no longer served (hard-refresh test).
5. Rotate every other secret that may have been stored in the same account (S3 bucket keys, DB passwords, API tokens), since an attacker with root could have exfiltrated them.

**Short term (within days):**

6. Do not use the root user for day-to-day operations. Create a dedicated IAM (or IAM Identity Center) user with least-privilege permissions and use that from here on.
7. Enable AWS GuardDuty and billing anomaly alerts to detect reuse of leaked credentials or sudden spend changes.
8. Add a secret-scanning gate to the deployment pipeline (e.g., gitleaks, trufflehog) so no commit containing `AKIA`/`ASIA`/AWS secret patterns can be released.
9. Any client-side code that needs to talk to AWS must use short-lived temporary credentials (Amazon Cognito, STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) — never a long-lived root key.

**Long term:**

10. Adopt a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault) for all backend secrets; never ship secrets in client-side JavaScript regardless of comment status, because every byte sent to the browser is public.

data.title: Public S3 Bucket - All User Images (Including "Private") Are World-Readable and Enumerable
data.summary: The S3 bucket that stores every uploaded image for Imager is configured so that any person on the internet, with no credentials, can list every file and download any image - including images users explicitly marked as "Private". The platform's privacy promise does not match reality: there is effectively no such thing as a private image on Imager.
data.description:
Two anonymous (unauthenticated) HTTP requests were made directly to the bucket:

1. `GET https://filesharer-research.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2` -> HTTP 200. Response is a standard `ListBucketResult` XML containing all 49 object keys at the time of testing. Each key follows the pattern `users/<user_uuid>/<image_uuid>.<ext>`, revealing all user IDs and all image IDs stored in the system.
2. `GET https://filesharer-research.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/users/0c3f8747-73f2-4f1f-b453-010f5b7fa950/925e5bda-6b04-4dfb-9b92-d557da791d57.jpg` -> HTTP 200, Content-Type image/jpeg, 628 bytes of valid JPEG data. This object was a PRIVATE image uploaded by test Account B during authorization-flow testing; it was fetched without any credentials, cookies, or signed URL.

**Additional observations.**

- 22 distinct `user_<uuid>/` directories were enumerated with a single request.
- Several directory names contained invalid characters (`"`, `'`, empty string, and arbitrary text) — a direct consequence of the upload mass-assignment IDOR (separate finding), which has clearly been exercised in the wild and polluted the bucket keyspace.
- Anonymous PUT and DELETE were correctly rejected (HTTP 403); the bucket is READ-ONLY to the public, not writable.

**Business impact.** Full confidentiality loss for every image ever uploaded. Private images are not private. Privacy / Notifiable Data Breach exposure under the Australian Privacy Act 1988 if any identifying content exists in user images. Legal and reputational risk: Imager's "your images, your control" tagline is directly contradicted by this misconfiguration. Attackers can enumerate all user UUIDs and correlate them with the public-facing `/images/<uuid>` URL space to systematically harvest content. Combined with the IDOR findings and the leaked AWS root key, an attacker has multiple independent paths to the same data.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p2-s3-and-enum/s3list.xml`, `s3all.xml` (anonymous ListBucket)
- `evidence/p2-s3-and-enum/retry/list.xml`, `obj-*.bin` (anonymous image downloads)
- `evidence/p2-final/p1-fetch.*` (private image fetched anonymously)
data.recommendation:
**Immediate:**

1. Enable AWS "Block Public Access" at both the account and bucket level on `filesharer-research` (ap-southeast-2): S3 Console -> Buckets -> filesharer-research -> Permissions -> Block public access -> enable all 4 settings.
2. Review the bucket policy and object ACLs; remove any `Principal: "*"` or `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers` grants.
3. Serve images via a signed URL mechanism that requires an authentication check inside Imager's application (the app already generates pre-signed URLs — it just needs the bucket to default-deny unsigned requests).
4. Rotate any sensitive data that may have been exposed; notify affected users as required by the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme if any PII-bearing images are in the bucket.

**Short term:**

5. Shorten the pre-signed URL `X-Amz-Expires` from 604800 seconds (7 days) to the minimum operationally required (5-15 minutes).
6. Add CloudTrail and GuardDuty monitoring for S3 bucket activity. Alert on anonymous requests and on mass `GetObject` patterns.
7. Enable S3 Server Access Logging (or CloudTrail data events) and review the last 90 days for signs that external parties have already enumerated the bucket.
8. Decide and apply a key-naming policy that does NOT embed trust in client-provided fields (`user_id`). Prefer server-generated, random keys stored and resolved via the database.

data.title: PostgreSQL Database Server Exposed to the Public Internet
data.summary: The database powering imagesharer.xyz is reachable from any address on the public internet. The application and the database are co-located on the same server, so no external party has a legitimate reason to connect to port 5432. The open port creates a direct path for attackers to attempt credential guessing, exploit PostgreSQL vulnerabilities, and (if they obtain credentials) steal, modify, or destroy all image and user data.
data.description:
A targeted service probe to 51.161.131.44 TCP/5432 returned:

```
PORT     STATE SERVICE    VERSION
5432/tcp open  postgresql PostgreSQL DB
Protocol: 3.0 (confirmed via PostgreSQL error response)
TLS on 5432: not configured
```

The service accepts arbitrary TCP connections from the internet. No authentication attempt was made (out of scope per rules of engagement), but the exposure alone materially increases risk:

- Any attacker, including unattended internet-wide scanners, can connect and attempt to authenticate.
- Credential guessing against `pg_hba.conf`'s `md5` / `scram-sha-256` is possible at scale.
- Historical PostgreSQL CVEs (RCE, authentication bypass, privilege escalation) are reachable before they can be patched.
- Data is transmitted in cleartext because TLS is not enforced on the port.

**Business impact.** A single stolen or guessed database password equals full loss of user data (images, usernames, password hashes, email addresses, sessions). Compliance implications under the Australian Privacy Act / Notifiable Data Breaches scheme if real user data is accessed.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p0-postgres/nmap-5432.txt`
data.recommendation:
**Immediate:**

1. Restrict TCP/5432 at the firewall. Simplest fixes on OVH:
   - Edit `postgresql.conf`: `listen_addresses = 'localhost'` and restart PostgreSQL. The web app on the same server will still connect via 127.0.0.1.
   - If a separate DB host is needed, allow 5432 only from the application's IP in `pg_hba.conf` AND restrict with ufw/iptables / OVH security group.
2. Verify no PostgreSQL password uses `postgres`, `password`, `admin`, or an empty value. Rotate the application's DB user password to a long, randomly generated secret.

**Short term:**

3. Enable TLS on PostgreSQL (`ssl = on`) with a valid certificate, and require `hostssl` entries in `pg_hba.conf`.
4. Enable `pg_hba.conf` method `scram-sha-256` (not `md5`) for all users.
5. Keep PostgreSQL packages patched (currently ambiguous on-wire version — ensure latest 16.x LTS).
6. Add fail2ban or equivalent to lock out hosts after repeated failed PostgreSQL logins.

data.title: Mass Assignment / IDOR on Image Upload (Attacker Uploads Images to Any Victim Account)
data.summary: When a signed-in Imager user uploads a picture, the upload form includes a hidden `user_id` field that identifies who owns the image. The server trusts whatever value the browser sends in that field instead of using the authenticated session. Any logged-in user can paste another member's user ID into the request and the picture is saved as if the other member uploaded it - appearing on their dashboard, counted against their quota, and attributed to them in any audit log.
data.description:
Upload page HTML (`/images/upload`) includes:

```html
<input name="user_id" type="hidden" value="<caller's own UUID>">
<input name="file" type="file" required>
<input name="is_public" type="radio" ...>
```

**Reproduction (verified):**

1. Account A (UUID `c9178440-59d6-4715-b8dc-782c592c5885`) was authenticated via `PHPSESSID`.
2. Multipart `POST /images/upload` with field `user_id` = Account B's UUID (`0c3f8747-73f2-4f1f-b453-010f5b7fa950`).
3. Server returned HTTP 302 `Location: /images/ed9b9ab1-b69c-40a7-a2eb-3582f889a67c`.
4. Account B's dashboard (fetched independently) now shows image `ed9b9ab1-b69c-40a7-a2eb-3582f889a67c` as owned by B, even though B never uploaded it.

Full raw request/response captured in `evidence/p2-uploads/idor/`.

**Business impact.** An attacker can plant content on any victim's account. For an image-sharing platform this is severe: an attacker can plant unlawful or defamatory images under a known user's name, exposing that user (and Imagur) to legal, reputational, and law-enforcement consequences. In the worst case, Imagur itself may be served with takedown notices for content it believes a specific user chose to upload. The defect can also be used to exhaust a user's storage quota (per-user DoS) or spam a victim's gallery. The forensic trail is destroyed: logs will say "User B uploaded X" when in fact User A did.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p2-uploads/idor/baseline.body`, `baseline.headers`
- `evidence/p2-uploads/idor/idor.body`, `idor.headers`
- `evidence/p2-uploads/idor/dash-a.html`, `dash-b.html`
data.recommendation:
1. Remove the hidden `user_id` field from the HTML form entirely — the browser cannot be trusted to tell the server which user is logged in.
2. In the upload handler, derive the owning `user_id` SOLELY from the authenticated session (e.g., `$_SESSION['user_id']`). Discard any `user_id` value that arrives in the POST body.
3. Add an integration test: as user A, submit a crafted multipart POST with `user_id` = user B. Assert the stored row's owner matches A.
4. Review every other endpoint that takes an entity ID in the body for the same pattern (`POST /profile/avatar`, `POST /logout`, `POST /images/{id}/visibility` — see separate finding).
5. Consider migrating to a framework-level pattern (e.g., Laravel's `$request->user()` / policies) that makes it hard to accidentally trust client-supplied owner IDs.

data.title: Broken Access Control on Image Visibility Toggle (IDOR - Attacker Makes a Victim's Private Image Public)
data.summary: Any logged-in user who knows (or guesses from an email, dashboard link, or shared URL) another user's image ID can switch that image from "private" to "public" without owning it. Private images are therefore not reliably private: a single HTTP request from another member exposes them to the open internet.
data.description:
**Reproduction (verified):**

1. Account B uploaded a PRIVATE image (ID `925e5bda-6b04-4dfb-9b92-d557da791d57`).
2. Account A sent `POST /images/925e5bda-6b04-4dfb-9b92-d557da791d57/visibility` with body `is_public=true`, authenticated as A.
3. Server responded HTTP 302 to the image detail page (success flow).
4. Account B's dashboard subsequently displayed the image as Public without B taking any action.

The server does not check that the authenticated user owns the image before changing a sensitive property. The same pattern on the delete endpoint was observed to be correctly gated (image remained after A's attempt), confirming an authorization check exists in the code base — it simply was not applied here.

**Business impact.** Direct violation of the user's privacy expectation ("Private = only you"). A malicious or compromised account can run through every image UUID it learns about (shared links, scraping public pages, leaked log data) and silently flip them to public. The now-public image is retrievable via its `/images/<uuid>` page AND via a long-lived S3 pre-signed URL (see separate finding). Combined with the image upload IDOR, an attacker can plant an image on a victim's account AND make it public, then advertise the URL — a credible content-planting plus exposure attack.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p2-authz/authz-tests.log`
- `evidence/p2-authz/s3.headers`, `s3.body`
data.recommendation:
1. In the visibility handler, SELECT the image row and verify `image.owner_id == $_SESSION['user_id']` BEFORE applying the update. Return HTTP 403/404 otherwise.
2. Apply the same explicit ownership check to every `/images/<uuid>/*` endpoint. Treat the per-image delete endpoint as the reference implementation and extend the same pattern.
3. Add server-side logging and alerting when an ownership check fails. Repeated failures from one session are a strong IDOR-probing signal.
4. Add a regression test: user A tries to change visibility of a UUID owned by B — expect 403/404 and no DB mutation.

data.title: Private Images Expose Long-Lived Pre-signed URLs That Bypass "Private" Status
data.summary: When the owner of a PRIVATE image opens its detail page, Imager inserts an AWS S3 pre-signed URL into the HTML - including a "Direct link" field users may copy. This URL is a bearer token that works for anyone, from anywhere, for 7 full days, regardless of whether the image remains private. If a user shares the URL once (messaging, screenshot, log file, help ticket, browser history export), the "private" image is effectively public for a week.
data.description: **Reproduction (verified):** 1. Account A uploaded a PRIVATE image (ID `4cbfdbb9-52f1-42e4-ba95-33b32e40ec2b`). 2. Account A opened `/images/4cbfdbb9-52f1-42e4-ba95-33b32e40ec2b`. The HTML included: - An `` element. - A "Direct link" `` containing the same signed URL for easy copying. 3. The signed URL was taken out-of-band and fetched with no session cookie, no referrer, from an unrelated client -> HTTP 200, image/jpeg, full image bytes. 4. The `X-Amz-Expires=604800` parameter indicates the URL is valid for 7 days regardless of subsequent visibility changes on the Imager side. *Note: This finding is independent of the public-bucket finding. Even if the bucket is correctly locked down, pre-signed URLs remain valid, by design of AWS, until expiry.* **Business impact.** Users have a strong, implicit expectation that "Private" means "nobody else can view this". That contract is broken. A single accidental URL share leaks the image for 7 days, and the URL cannot be revoked individually. Combined with the public bucket, the attack surface is large; fixing one does not fix the other. **Evidence.** `evidence/p2-final/p1-up.*`, `p1-detail.html`, `p1-fetch.*`
data.recommendation:
1. Do NOT render pre-signed URLs for private images on the owner's detail page. Instead, serve a server-mediated endpoint such as `GET /images/<uuid>/raw`, which checks session + ownership + current visibility on every request and streams the file.
2. If pre-signed URLs are retained for public images, cap `X-Amz-Expires` to the minimum operationally required (default 300 seconds). Never 7 days.
3. If a user toggles a public image to private, immediately rotate / overwrite the object (or set a new object key) so any outstanding pre-signed URL stops working.
4. Add a user-visible "Rotate link" button so owners can invalidate the current direct link on demand.
affected_components: GET https://imagesharer.xyz/images/<uuid> (owner view for PRIVATE images)

data.title: Production Application Also Exposed Over Plaintext HTTP on Port 8080
data.summary: The Imager application is served not only over HTTPS on port 443 (via imagesharer.xyz) but also over PLAINTEXT HTTP on port 8080 directly on the server's IP. Anyone visiting http://51.161.131.44:8080/ gets the real, logged-in, interactive production application without TLS. If a user signs in that way (or is tricked into clicking such a link), their email, password, session cookie, and uploaded images traverse the network in the clear and can be captured by anyone on the same network path.
data.description:
- `curl http://51.161.131.44:8080/login` returns the identical "Log in — Imager" HTML as the HTTPS site (byte-identical body).
- The same `/js/awsvalid.js` (containing the leaked AWS root credential) is served from this port.
- The server does NOT redirect port 8080 to HTTPS and does NOT reject plaintext requests.
- There is no vhost gating (Host header does not affect behavior).
- Nothing on the production site advertises port 8080, so it is unlikely to be used by legitimate users — but it is reachable by any scanner on the internet and by any attacker who crafts a link.

**Business impact.** Session hijacking, credential theft, and image theft for any user who authenticates over port 8080. Phishing lure: an attacker who sends `http://51.161.131.44:8080/login?return=...` can intercept credentials in a controlled MITM/relay setup. Weakens the security story: Imager appears HTTPS-only to the end user, but the backend is reachable in cleartext.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p3-infra/other-ports/*` and `port8080/*` (banner, title, awsvalid.js, side-by-side hashing)
data.recommendation:
1. Close port 8080 at the OS or OVH firewall. If the port is only needed for internal process-manager health checks, bind the Apache listener to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0`.
2. If port 8080 must remain publicly reachable (e.g., for a load balancer that cannot be reconfigured right now), make it serve ONLY a permanent HTTPS redirect to `https://imagesharer.xyz/`, and set `Strict-Transport-Security` on the HTTPS response (see Headers finding) so browsers remember HTTPS.
3. Audit the server for any other Apache/nginx vhost listening on non-443 ports; apply the same policy.

data.title: Dangling / Misconfigured CloudFront Alias on resources.imagesharer.xyz
data.summary: Imagur's DNS points `resources.imagesharer.xyz` to an AWS CloudFront distribution that is not configured to accept that hostname. Browsers requesting the URL see a security warning (the TLS certificate does not cover the hostname), and the distribution returns HTTP 403 for every request. The intended behavior (serving the site's favicon from `https://resources.imagesharer.xyz/icon.ico`) is broken. The state also leaves a smaller risk of future takeover if the CloudFront distribution is ever deleted while the DNS record remains.
data.description:
**Observed:**

- DNS: `resources.imagesharer.xyz CNAME d273uevi0662l0.cloudfront.net`
- TLS (SNI `resources.imagesharer.xyz`): certificate `CN=*.cloudfront.net`, SANs `*.cloudfront.net`, `cloudfront.net` only — DOES NOT include `resources.imagesharer.xyz`, so every browser request raises a certificate error.
- HTTP: 403 Forbidden on both `/` and `/icon.ico` with headers `Server: CloudFront` and `X-Cache: Error from cloudfront`, confirming the distribution exists but does not have `resources.imagesharer.xyz` listed as an alternate domain name (CNAME alias).
- Direct access to `d273uevi0662l0.cloudfront.net` reveals an origin of AmazonS3 (empty 404), meaning the origin bucket is either empty or unconfigured.
- The main login page references this hostname (favicon), so any user who views page source or any future dependency on this host will encounter broken resources and TLS warnings — degrading trust and triggering browser phishing-detection heuristics on some clients.

**Takeover risk.** If the CloudFront distribution is ever deleted (common during cost cleanup) and the DNS CNAME is not removed, a different AWS customer could set up a CloudFront alias for `resources.imagesharer.xyz` and serve content from it. The present risk is low (the distribution is active), but it will materialize the moment the distribution is deleted.

**Business impact.** Broken intended functionality (favicon / static assets). Loss of user trust if any URL is shared publicly (browser certificate warning page). Latent subdomain-takeover risk if the distribution is ever deprovisioned.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p0-cloudfront/cloudfront-check.txt`
data.recommendation:
Choose ONE:

**A) If the CDN subdomain is still needed:**

1. In the CloudFront distribution (`d273uevi0662l0.cloudfront.net`) -> Settings -> Alternate domain names (CNAMEs), add `resources.imagesharer.xyz`.
2. Request a public ACM certificate (us-east-1) for `resources.imagesharer.xyz` and attach it to the distribution.
3. Confirm the S3 origin bucket contains the expected content (icon.ico, static assets) and that Origin Access Control is correctly configured.

**B) If the CDN subdomain is NOT needed:**

1. Delete the `resources.imagesharer.xyz` CNAME record at the DNS provider (Spaceship).
2. Remove the (commented) HTML reference in the login page.

**C) General:**

3. Document a rule in deployment / off-boarding checklists: never delete a CloudFront distribution or S3 bucket without first removing or re-pointing the DNS record that points to it.

data.title: Weak Password Policy - Single-Character Passwords Accepted
data.summary: The registration form claims to require passwords of 8 characters or more, but this check is enforced only in the browser (HTML `minlength=8`). A direct HTTP POST with a one-character password is accepted and the account is created with that one-character password. Users following the UI get a reasonable policy; attackers who send raw requests get none.
data.description:
**Observed:**

- Legitimate flow via browser: `minlength=8` enforced client-side; UX gated.
- Direct POST: `curl -X POST -d 'email=weakpw-test@test.local&password=a&confirm=a' https://imagesharer.xyz/register` -> HTTP 302 (success response).

The companion issue was also tested: mismatched `password` and `confirm` fields are NOT enforced server-side either; the password is set to whatever `password` contains and `confirm` is cosmetic.

**Business impact.** Any user who registers via API, test harness, mobile client, or scripted sign-up can establish an account whose password is trivial to guess. When combined with the lack of rate limiting on `/login` (separate finding) and the user-enumeration on `/register` (separate finding), credential stuffing / targeted password guessing becomes very cheap.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p2-misc/p4.body`, `p4.headers` (1-char password accepted)
- `evidence/p2-misc/p5.body`, `p5.headers` (confirm mismatch accepted)
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce the password policy server-side (minimum 8 characters, mix of character classes OR length >= 12 — follow NIST 800-63B).
2. Server-side validate `password === confirm` and reject with HTTP 400 otherwise.
3. Check new passwords against a well-known breached-password list (e.g., HaveIBeenPwned k-anonymity API).
4. Return explicit, actionable validation errors so legitimate users can self-correct.

data.title: No Rate Limiting on /login (Enables Credential Brute Force)
data.summary: Failed login attempts are not rate-limited. Five consecutive wrong-password attempts in rapid succession all returned the same `302 -> /login` response with no 429, no CAPTCHA, no account lockout, no exponential backoff. An attacker can therefore attempt thousands of passwords per second against a known email without obstruction.
data.description:
Five rapid POSTs to `/login` with the real test email and five different wrong passwords all returned HTTP 302 immediately (sub-200 ms each). No throttling observed.

**Business impact.** Online password guessing against known-good emails (which the registration-enumeration finding makes easy to collect) is feasible. Combined with the weak-password-policy finding (users may have 1-character passwords), compromise is realistic. Credential stuffing with leaked-password datasets costs essentially nothing to run.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p2-final/final-tests.log` (R-1 section)
data.recommendation:
1. Rate-limit `/login` by (IP + email) key: for example, after 5 failures in 15 minutes, respond with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` header for 15 minutes.
2. Add exponential backoff / login-captcha after the second failure within a short window.
3. Alert on sustained high failure rates per IP range for operational awareness.
4. Prefer a WebAuthn / passkey option so password brute force is simply not applicable.

data.title: Open DNS Resolver on Port 53 (Potential DDoS Amplification Reflector)
data.summary: The server is running an open DNS resolver that recursively answers queries from anyone on the internet. The server returned a correct answer when asked to resolve `example.com` from an unrelated source address. Open resolvers are routinely abused as reflectors in DDoS amplification attacks: an attacker spoofs a victim's IP, sends a small query, and the resolver sends a large reply to the victim. Imager's server would be the unwitting attacker in such an incident, leading to IP reputation damage, upstream provider complaints, and potential service degradation while the DDoS traffic is sourced from this host.
data.description:
- `dig @51.161.131.44 example.com +short` returned Cloudflare IPs for example.com, confirming full recursive resolution for an off-domain query.
- `version.bind CHAOS TXT` and `hostname.bind CHAOS TXT` were blocked / returned no useful banner — good.
- Direct impact to Imagur is modest, but reputational and operational exposure is real: upstream (OVH) may null-route the host under abuse complaint; the server contributes to internet-wide DDoS.

**Business impact.** Potential upstream null-route by OVH if the server is reported in a DDoS incident. Resource consumption during amplification abuse (bandwidth, CPU). Reputational: Imagur's IP may land on abuse databases, affecting outbound mail or API callbacks later.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p3-infra/other-ports/probe-other.log`
data.recommendation:
1. If this server is not supposed to be a DNS server, STOP the resolver daemon (bind9/unbound/dnsmasq/systemd-resolved) or bind it to `127.0.0.1` only.
2. If it must run DNS, restrict recursion with ACLs:
   - BIND: `allow-recursion { 127.0.0.1; <trusted-ranges>; };`
   - Unbound: `access-control: 0.0.0.0/0 refuse` then allow specific ranges.
3. Add rate limiting (`rate-limit { responses-per-second 5; };` in BIND) as defense-in-depth.
4. Verify the fix publicly via https://openresolverproject.org/ or `dig @51.161.131.44 example.com` from an off-net client.

data.title: User-Enumeration via Registration Endpoint
data.summary: When a visitor attempts to register an email that is already in use, Imager replies with the explicit message "An account with that email already exists.". Attackers can therefore test any email against the site and learn whether that person has an Imager account. (For comparison, the `/login` endpoint correctly returns the same message for both unknown-email and wrong-password cases - this is good; `/register` must be aligned with that behaviour.)
data.description:
Verified with explicit POST + follow-up GET of `/register` as the same session. Known-registered email yields `"An account with that email already exists."`. Unknown emails produce the normal signup success flow. The login endpoint returns an identical `"Invalid email or password."` for both wrong-password and unknown-email (good — do not change this).

**Business impact.** Enables attackers to confirm whether specific individuals have accounts, which supports targeted phishing, social engineering, and credential stuffing campaigns. Enables bulk account mapping from a list of email addresses.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p2-s3-and-enum/retry/getC.html` (quoted error)
- `evidence/p2-s3-and-enum/retry/getA.html`, `getB.html` (login — identical)
data.recommendation:
1. On `/register`, do NOT reveal whether the email is already registered. Return a generic success message and send an email to the address: either (a) a verification email if new, or (b) a "someone tried to re-register this address" notice if already present. The flow is unchanged for legitimate owners; attackers get no signal.
2. Combine with CAPTCHA + registration rate limiting (per IP, per email) to raise the cost of bulk enumeration.

data.title: Unhandled Server Error on Empty user_id Parameter (Denial via Malformed Input)
data.summary: When an authenticated user submits an image upload with an empty `user_id` field, the server returns an HTTP 500 `INTERNAL_ERROR` instead of a validated HTTP 400 Bad Request. This indicates a missing input-validation path and leaks information about internal state.
data.description:
**Request:** `POST /images/upload` with `user_id=&file=<jpeg>&is_public=false`, cookie present.
**Response:** HTTP 500 with an `INTERNAL_ERROR` body.

While minor on its own, this is diagnostic evidence that the upload handler trusts client input blindly (consistent with the mass-assignment IDOR finding) and lacks defensive validation.

**Business impact.** Minor information disclosure (presence of an unhandled branch). Each triggering request wastes server resources.

**Evidence.** `evidence/p2-final/u2.h`, `u2.b`
data.recommendation:
1. Remove the `user_id` form field entirely (see the Mass Assignment finding). Once removed, this error path no longer applies.
2. Add a generic request-validation layer that returns HTTP 400 for any missing/invalid required fields and never returns 500 for user-controllable input.
3. Ensure production error responses do not disclose stack traces, class names, or framework internals.

data.title: Missing HTTP Security Headers (HSTS, CSP) and Email Anti-Spoofing (SPF, DMARC)
data.summary: Several low-cost hardening headers and DNS records are missing. Each on its own is minor, but together they weaken defense-in-depth against TLS downgrade attacks, cross-site scripting, and email spoofing.
data.description:
**Observed on `https://imagesharer.xyz/`:**

- `Strict-Transport-Security`: NOT SET -> browsers can be downgraded to HTTP on a hostile network before the first HTTPS visit of a session.
- `Content-Security-Policy`: NOT SET -> no second-layer defense against XSS; inline scripts, inline event handlers, and arbitrary CDN origins are permitted.
- `Permissions-Policy`: NOT SET -> no restrictions on camera/microphone/geolocation APIs if ever abused by a stored XSS.
- `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` / `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`: NOT SET.

**Observed in DNS for `imagesharer.xyz`:**

- `MX` records: NONE present.
- `SPF` (`TXT v=spf1`): NOT present.
- `DMARC` (`TXT _dmarc.imagesharer.xyz`): NOT present.
- `CAA`: NOT present.

The domain can therefore be freely spoofed as a sender in email, since there is no SPF `-all` / `v=spf1 -all` policy and no DMARC `reject` policy. Attackers can send mail "from" `help@imagesharer.xyz` with high deliverability.

**Business impact.** Easier for attackers to run convincing phishing / password-reset lures that appear to come from Imager. No protection against TLS downgrade for first-time visitors on hostile networks (cafe wifi, hotels, airport). No browser-level containment should a stored XSS appear anywhere in the application.

**Evidence.**

- `evidence/p1-discovery/root.headers.txt`
- Enumeration YAML (`dns_infrastructure` / `mail_infrastructure` sections)
data.recommendation:
1. Add response headers at the nginx layer:
   - `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`
   - `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://filesharer-research.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'self'`
   - `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`
2. Add DNS records at Spaceship DNS:
   - `imagesharer.xyz. TXT "v=spf1 -all"` (or `-all` plus the real sending host if mail will be sent).
   - `_dmarc.imagesharer.xyz. TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:security@imagesharer.xyz"`
   - `imagesharer.xyz. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` to pin which CAs may issue certificates.
3. After HSTS has been live for >= 6 months with no issues, submit the domain to the HSTS preload list.

data.title: SSH (OpenSSH 10.0p2) Exposed to the Public Internet
data.summary: SSH is open to the entire internet. This is extremely common for small cloud VPSes but still represents an unnecessary attack surface. There is nothing immediately exploitable in the OpenSSH banner (10.0p2 is current), but any future SSH CVE or any weak password / credential leak becomes directly exploitable from anywhere.
data.description: Nmap banner: `22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 10.0p2 Debian 7+deb13u4 (protocol 2.0)`. No evidence of banner suppression; no attempt was made (nor permitted) to authenticate.
data.recommendation:
Defense in depth, not urgent:

1. Restrict SSH to the administrator's IP / VPN at the OVH firewall or via `AllowUsers` / `Match Address` in `sshd_config`.
2. Disable password authentication (`PasswordAuthentication no`) and allow only public-key auth.
3. Disable root login (`PermitRootLogin no` or `prohibit-password`).
4. Install `fail2ban` and set `MaxAuthTries 3` to deter online guessing.
5. Keep OpenSSH patched promptly (automated apt-upgrade or unattended-upgrades).
